tip: lekker means much more than tasty. Slaap lekker means sleep well, and lekker adds a pleasant, comfortable feel to all sorts of activities.
gezellig has no single English match. It blends cozy, sociable, and enjoyable, here saying the gathering was warm and fun.
vlakbij means right nearby, stronger than dichtbij, and takes its object directly: vlakbij de school.
After een with a het-word, the adjective drops its -e: een moeilijk probleem, not moeilijke, because probleem is a het-word.
Start a sentence with zojuist and the verb comes before the subject: zojuist heb ik, not zojuist ik heb.
groot loses one o and adds -e before a noun: een grote boom. The double vowel shortens to one in the open syllable.
van shows possession here: de brief is van mijn broer means the letter is my brother's. Dutch has no 's ending for this.
vanwege means because of and takes a noun: vanwege wegwerkzaamheden. Use omdat instead when a full clause follows.
ontbijten is a verb meaning to eat breakfast, so wij ontbijten needs no extra verb like the English have.
onder de brug door adds door at the end to show moving all the way under, not just resting under the bridge.
wegleggen splits in a command: leg je telefoon weg, with weg jumping to the end of the clause.
Add -er to form the comparative: moeilijk becomes moeilijker for more difficult.
Dutch chooses staat for upright things: een glas staat op de tafel, where English just says the glass is on the table.
For something situated flat or spread out Dutch uses ligt: de tuin ligt achter het gebouw, the garden lies behind it.
Put het before an infinitive to turn it into a noun: het werken means the working, the activity itself.
The superlative adds -ste and pairs with het: het veiligste fietspad, the safest bike path.
verstaan means to catch or hear words, not grasp meaning. Ik versta je niet means I cannot make out what you say.
anderhalf is one single word for one and a half: anderhalf uur means an hour and a half.
blijven plus an infinitive means to keep doing something: ik bleef werken means I kept on working.
om ... te pairs a verb with an infinitive: besloot om te beginnen means decided to start.
Dutch marks transport with met: met de auto means by car, literally with the car.
er plus a verb introduces existence: er werken hier mensen means people work here. English drops this er.
A short adjective doubles its final consonant before -e: nat becomes natte in het natte gras.
Clock times take om: om vijf uur means at five o'clock.
After waarom the verb moves to the end: waarom zij zo boos was, not waarom zij was boos.
over means across an open surface: over het plein means across the square.
wachten takes op for waiting for something: wachten op de trein means to wait for the train.
opstaan splits in a main clause: ik sta ... op, with op sent to the very end.
With sinds Dutch keeps the present tense: ik woon sinds twee jaar means I have lived here for two years.
Dutch uses zit for something seated or tucked in: de kat zit onder de stoel.
Use elk with het-words and elke with de-words: elk weekend but elke week.
The accents in één mark it as the number one and stress it: met één hand means with just one hand.
uitnodigen can split far apart: nodigen wraps the whole middle and uit lands at the very end of the clause.
liever means would rather or prefer to: blijven wij liever binnen means we would rather stay inside.
goed has an irregular comparative: beter, not goeder. Een betere oplossing means a better solution.
After a voiceless sound the past tense adds -te, not -de: maken becomes maakte.
die is the relative pronoun for de-words: een hond die Max heette means a dog that was called Max.
A modal like moet pushes the main verb to the end: moet ... opladen means must top up.
